title: the dice game
hook: stake after stake, the same short line: I have won; and Vidura warns that the winner is in danger too

segments.voice: Yesterday, the talk before the first throw: a warning, a dare, a vow, and a pearl set in gold, lost. Ask whose voice that is.
screen: `CALLED TO PLAY, I DON'T TURN BACK.`

segments.voice: There's a line in this part of the poem that keeps coming back, like a drumbeat. Yudhishthira names a stake. Shakuni throws. And then Shakuni says, in effect: I have won. Then again. And again. The poem repeats it until the words themselves begin to sound like a warning. And one man in the hall stands up and tries to stop it.
screen: `A LINE LIKE A DRUMBEAT.` → `I HAVE WON.` → `ONE MAN TRIES TO STOP IT.`

segments.voice: After the pearl, Yudhishthira reaches for the next stake. Treasure. Gold. A fine chariot. Servants. Elephants. Horses. Soldiers. Each time he describes what he's putting down, carefully, almost proudly, as if the quality of the stake could change the fall of the dice. Each time the throw goes to Shakuni, and the same short sentence follows: I have won. That refrain takes the suspense away. We stop asking who will win the throw, and start asking something harder: why doesn't he stop? Somebody in the hall asks it out loud. Vidura, the blind king's wise half-brother, turns to Dhritarashtra. In the telling, he gives him a picture. A man climbs high after honey, so taken with the honey that he doesn't see the fall in front of him. That, Vidura says, is your son with the dice. He begs the king to stop the game while there's still a family left to save. Duryodhana answers with scorn. He accuses Vidura of always speaking for the other side, against the very family that shelters him. And Dhritarashtra says nothing that stops the game. Here's what's striking. Vidura's honey picture isn't about Yudhishthira, the one losing. It's about Duryodhana, the one winning. In the poem's eyes, the winner is in danger too. Each throw won for him is a step nearer the edge, and he can't see it, because his hands are full of honey.
screen: `STAKE AFTER STAKE.` · `THE DRUMBEAT: I HAVE WON.` · `VIDURA: THE MAN WHO CLIMBS FOR HONEY.` · `DURYODHANA SCORNS THE WARNING.` · then, large: `THE WINNER IS IN DANGER TOO.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something that's been going your way lately: an argument, a streak, a race at work, a game on your phone. Gently look past the honey to the edge you might not be seeing, a person, a cost, an evening you haven't been home, without needing to fix anything. If you pray, you can bring that edge into your prayer; if not, simply breathe with it.
The dice game. Stake after stake, the same short line, I have won, and Vidura warning that the one who's winning is in danger too.
Your line: the dice game. Tomorrow, the stakes stop being things. That's day seven hundred sixty-eight.

howItsDone: Vidura's warnings in the dice hall are a place where teachers and storytellers often pause, and his image of the honey-gatherer is retold as a picture of desire that can't see its own danger.

fork.setup: you're Vidura. the game is going badly, and the blind king is listening. what do you do?
options: keep quiet; it isn't your game.
speak to the king and beg him to stop it.
fork.reveal: he gives Dhritarashtra the picture of a man reaching for honey who doesn't see the fall, and begs him to stop. Duryodhana scorns him, and the game goes on.

original.note: Sanskrit akṣa: a die, the piece thrown in the game.

what it means: a refrain that turns suspense into dread, and a warning aimed at the winner.
what a scholar hears: Vidura speaks to Dhritarashtra, not to the players, so the poem puts the power to stop the game with the blind king.

chat.says: In Vidura's honey story, who's the one in danger, the loser or the winner?
options: The winner: Duryodhana, so taken with winning that he can't see the fall.
The loser: Yudhishthira, climbing after treasure he keeps losing.
Shakuni, who throws the dice and might be caught out by the king.
chat.meaning: Vidura told the blind king his son was like a man after honey who can't see the fall. The one winning is in danger too.

Vidura.meaning: the blind king's half-brother and wise counselor

Dhritarashtra.meaning: the blind king of Hastinapura, Duryodhana's father

Shakuni.meaning: Duryodhana's uncle, a master at dice

Yudhishthira.meaning: eldest of the five Pandava brothers

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Dyuta Parva (Yudhishthira's successive stakes and Shakuni's refrain; Vidura's warning to Dhritarashtra, the honey-gatherer image; Duryodhana's rebuke of Vidura)
